title: Multivalent antiviral conjugates enhance activity against Influenza via cross-linking viruses
abstract: Abstract Long-acting drug–Fc conjugate (CD388) has emerged as a new class of antivirals against influenza A and B, yet the mechanisms governing how Fc conjugation reshapes small-molecule function remain undefined. Here we establish a programmable multivalent antiviral conjugates (AVCs) platform by click chemistry that enables flexible combination of valencies and conjugated drugs, allowing systematic interrogation of valency-dependent antiviral mechanisms. Using zanamivir as a model, mono-, di-, and trivalent zanamivir are conjugated with Fc, with trivalent zanamivir-Fc conjugates (AVC-Z3) exhibiting higher activity than lower-valent AVCs. AVC-Z3 induces inter-virion aggregation, thereby coupling blockade of viral entry with restriction of viral release. This cross-linking–mediated dual-stage inhibition represents a mechanistic shift from neuraminidase suppression to physical viral immobilization. Furthermore, trivalent peramivir-Fc conjugate (AVC-P3) is synthesised and exhibits stronger antiviral activity than AVC-Z3 in vitro, with much longer half-life in vivo than AVC-Z3, and CD388 with YTE mutation. The in vivo antivirus efficacy of AVC-P3 surpasses other AVCs, baloxavir, and CD388 in H1N1-, H3N2-, H5N1-, and influenza B-infection mice models. Together, our findings define ligand valency as a determinant of antiviral mechanism.

title: Hemorrhagic tracheitis associated with swine influenza virus in a show pig
abstract: A crossbred show pig from Oklahoma presented with respiratory distress, coughing, and culmination of rapid progression to death. Postmortem examination revealed segmental hemorrhagic tracheitis with luminal narrowing from submucosal hemorrhage and histopathology confirmed ulcerative tracheitis and bronchointerstitial pneumonia. Polymerase chain reaction detected swine influenza virus in both the trachea and lungs. Swine influenza virus is a recognized component of the porcine respiratory disease complex and its association with hemorrhagic tracheitis suggests a potential role in hemorrhagic tracheitis syndrome. This Oklahoma case highlights the need for greater awareness and surveillance of this underrecognized condition.
journal: Journal of Swine Health and Production

title: Antibodies targeting a conserved cryptic epitope at the influenza hemagglutinin head-stem interface via distinct binding modes
abstract: Influenza A virus continues to pose pandemic threats, as demonstrated by the recent global spread of highly pathogenic H5N1 strains. Consequently, the development and characterization of vaccines targeting zoonotic influenza subtypes have become a major focus of the field. In this study, we characterize two broadly reactive antibodies previously isolated from H5N1 vaccinees. Although they have distinct immunoglobulin germline gene usage and binding modes, cryo-EM analysis shows that both antibodies share a highly conserved cryptic epitope at the interface of the hemagglutinin (HA) head and stem domains. The antigenicity of this epitope is influenced by natural amino acid variation at residue 293 of HA subunit 1, and its access is facilitated by acid-induced conformational change of HA. Nevertheless, both antibodies are non-neutralizing and possess only marginal protective efficacy against seasonal and H5N1 viruses in vivo, thus representing suboptimal vaccine responses. Overall, our findings expand the interactions of cross-reactive antibodies with an under-characterized HA epitope and provide insights for next-generation influenza vaccine design.

title: Persistent influenza A RNA detection in a fatal pediatric case of influenza-associated encephalopathy
abstract: Influenza-associated encephalopathy (IAE) is a life-threatening complication of influenza. We report a case of a 9-year-old boy diagnosed with fulminant IAE. The patient received life-sustaining support, intensive immunomodulatory therapy, and antiviral therapy. Following an initial single dose of baloxavir marboxil, persistent influenza A (H3N2) RNA detection prompted a multi-targeted antiviral regimen (oseltamivir, baloxavir marboxil, peramivir, and onradivir) as salvage therapy. Nevertheless, influenza A RNA remained detectable for more than 1 month, potentially reflecting severe neurological injury, immunosuppression, and impaired airway clearance.
journal: Journal of Infection and Public Health

full_text: Article summary AI generated Seasonal influenza outbreaks exhibit significant variability in magnitude and timing across different regions, highlighting the need to understand the environmental factors influencing these patterns. This study found that rapid thermal transitions and deviations from long-term temperature norms are associated with increased influenza incidence in multiple cities, suggesting that these dynamics may provide valuable insights for predicting epidemic activity beyond traditional absolute temperature measures. Abstract Background Seasonal influenza outbreaks show strong temporal regularity, but their magnitude and timing vary across years and locations. This study examined whether thermal transition dynamics, in addition to absolute temperature, are associated with influenza incidence across contrasting climatic settings. Methods We conducted a retrospective multi-city analysis of Beijing, Tokyo, New York, London, and Sydney. City-specific climatological baselines were constructed from daily temperature records for 1965–2025 and compared with daily influenza incidence data for 2020–2025. Analyses considered long-term thermal seasonality, short-term temperature–incidence co-variation, temperature anomalies, daily temperature change (ΔT), and exploratory snowfall indicators. Results Descriptive analyses showed that increases in reported influenza incidence frequently coincided with rapid warming, delayed cooling, and larger departures from city-specific temperature baselines. In adjusted time-series analyses, ΔT remained associated with influenza incidence in several cities after accounting for seasonal structure and absolute temperature, although the direction and magnitude varied by city and lag period. Absolute temperature-anomaly magnitude showed less consistent independent associations, and the snowfall findings remained exploratory. Conclusions Thermal transition rate and deviation from long-term climatic norms may provide complementary information for describing the timing of influenza activity beyond absolute temperature alone. Because the analysis was observational and covered the COVID-19 pandemic period, the findings should be interpreted as temporal associations rather than causal effects. Further studies using longer influenza time series and additional environmental and surveillance covariates are needed. 1 Introduction Seasonal influenza exhibits a striking regularity across temperate regions, with recurrent outbreaks emerging during predictable periods of the year [1,2,3]. Despite this apparent seasonality, the magnitude, timing, and growth rate of influenza epidemics vary substantially across years and locations, even within the same climatic zone. Understanding the environmental drivers underlying this variability remains a central challenge in climate–health research. Ambient temperature has long been recognized as an important factor influencing respiratory virus transmission [2, 4, 5]. Experimental and epidemiological studies have demonstrated that lower temperatures can enhance viral stability, prolong aerosol persistence, and modulate host immune responses. However, empirical findings linking absolute temperature levels to influenza incidence have been inconsistent across regions and time periods. In many settings, similar winter mean temperatures are associated with markedly different epidemic intensities, suggesting that static climatic indicators alone may be insufficient to explain observed patterns. Recent work has increasingly emphasized the role of climatic variability and extremes, rather than mean conditions, in shaping health outcomes [6,7,8,9,10,11]. Rapid temperature fluctuations have been associated with excess mortality, cardiovascular events, and respiratory morbidity, pointing to the importance of short-term environmental stressors.Within this broader context, it is therefore relevant to examine whether influenza seasonality is associated not only with absolute temperature levels, but also with how quickly and irregularly environmental conditions change during seasonal transitions. In temperate climates, two transitional periods are particularly salient: the gradual cooling from late summer into autumn, and the warming phase from winter into spring. These periods are characterized by pronounced temperature gradients, increased day-to-day variability, and shifts in surface energy balance. Such conditions may plausibly generate transient mismatches between viral environmental stability and host physiological adaptation, potentially amplifying susceptibility at the population level, although this remains to be empirically validated. Yet, the epidemiological relevance of these thermal transition dynamics has received limited systematic investigation [6,7,8,9,10,11]. Recent influenza modeling studies have also examined stochastic epidemic dynamics and cross-country transmission-control patterns, highlighting the importance of dynamic processes and setting-specific heterogeneity [12, 13, 16]. Another climatic feature that has received comparatively little attention in influenza research is snowfall. Beyond its association with low temperature, snowfall represents a distinct physical process involving latent heat exchange and surface energy redistribution. Its potential relationship with short-term epidemic dynamics therefore warrants exploratory examination. However, snowfall has rarely been examined explicitly as a modifying factor in temperature–influenza relationships. This study addresses these gaps by examining seasonal thermal transition dynamics alongside absolute temperature, including rates of warming and cooling, departures from long-term climatic norms, and the occurrence of snowfall events. We conduct a multi-city analysis across five global metropolitan areas—Beijing, Tokyo, New York, London, and Sydney—spanning different climate regimes and both hemispheres. Using more than six decades of daily temperature records, we establish city-specific climatological baselines that characterize typical annual thermal cycles. These baselines provide a reference against which recent epidemic-period conditions can be evaluated. We then examine daily influenza-related incidence data from 2020 to 2025, a period that includes both seasonal influenza activity and the COVID-19 pandemic, focusing on within-city temporal associations rather than cross-national burden comparisons. By integrating long-term climate context with short-term epidemiological dynamics, this study aims to explore whether and to what extent rapid thermal transitions, delayed seasonal cooling, and temperature anomalies are associated with changes in epidemic activity, and whether snowfall events correspond to measurable changes in incidence trajectories. By examining influenza seasonality in relation to temperature transitions as well as static thermal conditions, this work explores a dynamic perspective on climate–epidemic interaction under increasing climatic variability. Such an approach may be increasingly relevant under conditions of growing climate variability, where traditional seasonal assumptions are progressively disrupted. 2 Methods 2.1 Study design and data sources This study employed a retrospective observational design integrating long-term climatological records with short-term epidemiological time series to examine within-city temporal associations between seasonal temperature dynamics and influenza incidence. The analytical objective was to characterize how thermal transition processes relate to epidemic dynamics, rather than to predict disease outcomes or estimate absolute disease burden. Five metropolitan areas—Beijing, Tokyo, New York, London, and Sydney—were selected to represent diverse climate regimes, geographic settings, and both hemispheres, while also providing sufficiently long and continuous meteorological and epidemiological records for the study period. Daily mean surface air temperature data spanning 1965–2025 were obtained from publicly available global meteorological datasets providing long-term, station-based observations. These data were used exclusively to characterize city-specific climatological patterns and were not aggregated across locations. Epidemiological incidence data from 2020 to 2025 were derived from harmonized public health surveillance sources and national reporting systems. Influenza cases constituted the epidemiological outcome analyzed in this study and were analyzed separately from COVID-19 cases. COVID-19 case counts were not included in the influenza incidence series. Given heterogeneity in surveillance intensity and reporting practices across regions and over time, analyses focused on relative temporal variation within each city rather than cross-city comparisons of absolute incidence levels. All meteorological and epidemiological data used in this study were obtained from publicly accessible, aggregate databases; no private or individual-level participant data were used. All analyses were conducted using transparent, reproducible statistical procedures implemented in Python-based scientific computing libraries. No machine learning or artificial intelligence models were employed. The overall analytical framework, comprising climatic baseline construction, seasonal dynamics assessment, and anomaly-based transition analysis, is summarized in Fig. 1. An overview of the selected study cities, their climate characteristics, and data coverage is provided in Table 1. The study period (2020–2025) coincides with the COVID-19 pandemic and associated non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs), which substantially altered influenza transmission, surveillance, and testing patterns. COVID-19 cases were not included in the influenza incidence series. Accordingly, associations observed during this period were interpreted within the pandemic-affected surveillance context rather than as influenza-specific causal effects of climatic exposure. 2.2 Long-term climatic baseline construction To establish a reference framework for typical seasonal thermal conditions, a long-term daily climatological baseline was constructed for each city using the full 1965–2025 temperature record. For each calendar day \(d\in \{1,\dots ,365\}\), the baseline temperature \(\overline{T}_{d}\) was defined as: where \({T}_{y,d}\) denotes the observed daily mean temperature on day \(d\) in year \(y\), and \({N}_{d}\) represents the number of years with available observations for that calendar day. This procedure yields a smooth, city-specific annual thermal profile representing expected seasonal conditions. The resulting climatological baseline serves as a reference against which short-term temperature deviations and anomalous thermal transitions during recent epidemic periods can be evaluated. The overall procedure for constructing city-specific long-term climatic baselines is summarized in Fig. 2. 2.3 Seasonal temperature transition metrics Short-term thermal transitions were quantified using the daily temperature change rate, defined as: where \({T}_{t}\) is the daily mean temperature on day \(t\). This metric captures the speed and direction of warming or cooling independently of absolute temperature level. To reduce high-frequency noise in epidemiological reporting, daily influenza incidence was smoothed using a centered 7-day moving average: nitial associations between temperature transition metrics and epidemic activity were assessed descriptively using Pearson correlation analysis, focusing on within-city temporal co-variation between thermal change rates and incidence patterns. Because both climatic and epidemiological variables exhibit strong seasonal structure, additional seasonality-adjusted time-series analyses were conducted as described in Section G (Fig. 3). 2.4 Temperature anomalies relative to climatological norms To assess departures from expected seasonal thermal conditions, daily temperature anomalies were calculated relative to the long-term climatological baseline. For each day \(t\), the temperature anomaly \({A}_{t}\) was defined as: where \(\overline{T}_{d\left( t \right)}\) denotes the baseline temperature corresponding to the calendar day of \(t\). Both signed anomalies and absolute anomaly magnitudes \(\mid {A}_{t}\mid \) were examined. The absolute anomaly was used as an indicator of the intensity of climatic deviation, independent of whether conditions were warmer or cooler than expected. Associations between temperature anomalies and influenza incidence were evaluated descriptively to examine whether unusual thermal conditions co-varied with epidemic activity. The derivation of temperature anomaly and thermal transition metrics and their linkage to incidence analysis are summarized in Fig. 4. Definitions of all climatic and epidemiological variables used in the analysis are summarized in Table 2. 2.5 Humidity as a complementary climatic variable To incorporate additional environmental context relevant to respiratory virus transmission, relative humidity (RH) was included as a complementary climatic variable in the analysis. Daily RH data for each city were obtained from the same meteorological data sources as temperature records and processed using identical temporal alignment procedures. To ensure consistency with temperature-based analyses, RH time series were smoothed using a centered 7-day moving average to reduce short-term variability associated with reporting noise. A long-term climatological baseline for RH was constructed using the full available historical record, analogous to the temperature baseline. Daily humidity anomalies were defined as deviations from the corresponding calendar-day climatological mean. Associations between RH, RH anomalies, and influenza incidence were assessed descriptively, focusing on within-city temporal co-variation rather than cross-city comparability. RH was included as a supporting environmental variable rather than as a primary explanatory variable or an estimate of an independent effect. 2.6 Snowfall as an environmental modifier Snowfall events were identified using binary indicators derived from meteorological records. Days with snowfall were marked as \({S}_{t}=1\), and all other days as \({S}_{t}=0\). Snowfall was examined as a modifying environmental indicator rather than as a primary explanatory variable. Rather than assuming a direct causal relationship, snowfall was treated as an exploratory environmental marker associated with seasonal progression, with particular attention to temporal changes in epidemic activity around snowfall events. 2.7 Statistical analysis and reproducibility To distinguish associations with thermal transitions from those attributable to shared seasonal patterns, adjusted time-series analyses were conducted separately for each city. Daily influenza case counts were modelled using Poisson log-linear regression with a log link. Model coefficients were estimated by maximum likelihood using iteratively reweighted least squares. The principal exposure variables were daily temperature change (ΔT) and absolute temperature-anomaly magnitude, which were evaluated in separate models at lags of 0, 7, 14, and 21 days. Lags were defined using exact calendar-day displacement rather than row displacement, thereby preventing observations separated by gaps in the seasonal surveillance records from being treated as consecutive days. Each model included the thermal exposure of interest, absolute daily temperature, two pairs of Fourier terms representing annual and semi-annual seasonal cycles, categorical influenza-season indicators, and day-of-week indicators. Temporal autocorrelation and heteroskedasticity were addressed using a heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent sandwich covariance matrix with a Bartlett kernel and a maximum lag of 21 days. Autocovariance contributions were restricted to observations from the same influenza season and separated by the corresponding number of consecutive calendar days. Adjusted rate ratios (RRs) were obtained by exponentiating the exposure coefficients and are reported with autocorrelation-consistent 95% confidence intervals and two-sided p values. The Benjamini–Hochberg procedure was applied across the lag-specific analyses to control the false discovery rate, with q < 0.05 considered statistically significant. A structured summary of the analytical components, input datasets, and corresponding outputs is provided in Table 3. 3 Results 3.1 Long-term climatic baselines across cities Across all five cities, the 60-year mean daily temperature profiles exhibit smooth, unimodal seasonal cycles characteristic of their respective climate regimes (Fig. 5a–e). Northern Hemisphere cities (Beijing, London, Sydney, New York, and Tokyo) display synchronized seasonal timing, with temperature minima in winter and maxima in summer, while Sydney exhibits an approximately 6-month phase shift consistent with its Southern Hemisphere location. Despite substantial differences in absolute temperature ranges—ranging from the continental amplitude observed in Beijing to the more moderate maritime profile of London—the long-term baselines within each city remain stable and regular. These climatological baselines provide a consistent reference against which short-term thermal deviations and epidemic-period dynamics can be evaluated. 3.2 Seasonal temperature–incidence co-variation (2020–2025) Across all cities, influenza incidence during 2020–2025 exhibits pronounced seasonal structure when plotted alongside daily temperature (Fig. 6a–e). Visual comparison shows that increases in incidence frequently coincide with seasonal transition periods, including autumnal cooling and early spring warming, although these descriptive patterns do not by themselves distinguish thermal-transition associations from shared seasonality. analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to understand how seasonal thermal transitions influence influenza incidence across multiple cities, addressing the challenge of identifying environmental drivers of variability in outbreak patterns.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study employed a retrospective observational design integrating long-term climatological records with short-term epidemiological time series, focusing on Beijing, Tokyo, New York, London, and Sydney from 1965–2025. Influenza cases were analyzed separately from COVID-19 cases, with daily incidence smoothed using a 7-day moving average.
analysis.methods: Daily influenza incidence was smoothed using a centered 7-day moving average to reduce high-frequency noise. Associations between temperature transition metrics and epidemic activity were assessed descriptively using Pearson correlation analysis, focusing on within-city temporal co-variation. Relative humidity was included as a complementary climatic variable, also smoothed using a 7-day moving average, and analyzed for within-city temporal co-variation.
analysis.main_results: Descriptive analyses showed that increases in reported influenza incidence frequently coincided with rapid warming, delayed cooling, and larger departures from city-specific temperature baselines. Absolute temperature-anomaly magnitude showed less consistent independent associations, and the snowfall findings remained exploratory.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that thermal transition rate and deviation from long-term climatic norms may provide complementary information for describing the timing of influenza activity beyond absolute temperature alone.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that thermal transition dynamics could inform improved surveillance and prediction models for influenza activity, particularly in pandemic-affected contexts where traditional measures may be less reliable.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study focused on relative temporal variation within each city rather than cross-city comparisons, and analyses were conducted within the context of pandemic-affected surveillance, which may limit generalizability. The evidence is moderate.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the relationship between seasonal thermal transitions and influenza incidence across multiple cities, highlighting the variability in outbreak patterns and the need to understand environmental influences. Using a retrospective observational design, the researchers integrated long-term climatological data with short-term epidemiological time series, analyzing Beijing, Tokyo, New York, London, and Sydney. Daily influenza incidence was smoothed using a 7-day moving average, and associations with temperature transition metrics were assessed descriptively. Results indicated that rapid warming, delayed cooling, and deviations from city-specific temperature baselines were frequently linked to increased influenza reports. The authors suggested that thermal transition rates and deviations from climatic norms may offer additional insights into influenza timing beyond absolute temperature. However, the study focused on relative variation within cities and considered the impact of pandemic-related changes in surveillance, which may affect the generalizability of findings. The evidence is moderate, as the study did not employ machine learning or AI models and relied on descriptive analyses.

elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者认为,热变化速率和与长期气候标准的偏离可能为描述流感活动时间提供补充信息,超越绝对温度单独的作用。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明,热变化动态可能有助于改进 监测 和流感活动的预测模型,特别是在大流行影响的背景下,传统测量方法可能不够可靠。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究关注的是每个城市内部的相对时间变化,而非跨城市比较,且分析是在大流行影响的 监测 背景下进行的,这可能限制其普遍适用性。证据强度为中等。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to understand how seasonal thermal transitions influence influenza incidence across multiple cities, addressing the challenge of identifying environmental drivers of variability in outbreak patterns.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study employed a retrospective observational design integrating long-term climatological records with short-term epidemiological time series, focusing on Beijing, Tokyo, New York, London, and Sydney from 1965–2025. Influenza cases were analyzed separately from COVID-19 cases, with daily incidence smoothed using a 7-day moving average.
analysis_en.methods: Daily influenza incidence was smoothed using a centered 7-day moving average to reduce high-frequency noise. Associations between temperature transition metrics and epidemic activity were assessed descriptively using Pearson correlation analysis, focusing on within-city temporal co-variation. Relative humidity was included as a complementary climatic variable, also smoothed using a 7-day moving average, and analyzed for within-city temporal co-variation.
analysis_en.main_results: Descriptive analyses showed that increases in reported influenza incidence frequently coincided with rapid warming, delayed cooling, and larger departures from city-specific temperature baselines. Absolute temperature-anomaly magnitude showed less consistent independent associations, and the snowfall findings remained exploratory.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that thermal transition rate and deviation from long-term climatic norms may provide complementary information for describing the timing of influenza activity beyond absolute temperature alone.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that thermal transition dynamics could inform improved surveillance and prediction models for influenza activity, particularly in pandemic-affected contexts where traditional measures may be less reliable.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study focused on relative temporal variation within each city rather than cross-city comparisons, and analyses were conducted within the context of pandemic-affected surveillance, which may limit generalizability. The evidence is moderate.

title_zh: 季节性热变化动态及流感 发病率 在多个城市中的表现
source_body_en: This study found that rapid thermal transitions and deviations from long-term temperature norms are associated with increased influenza incidence in multiple cities, suggesting that these dynamics may provide valuable insights for predicting epidemic activity beyond traditional absolute temperature measures. This study examined whether thermal transition dynamics, in addition to absolute temperature, are associated with influenza incidence across contrasting climatic settings. Methods We conducted a retrospective multi-city analysis of Beijing, Tokyo, New York, London, and Sydney. Results Descriptive analyses showed that increases in reported influenza incidence frequently coincided with rapid warming, delayed cooling, and larger departures from city-specific temperature baselines. Absolute temperature-anomaly magnitude showed less consistent independent associations, and the snowfall findings remained exploratory. Because the analysis was observational and covered the COVID-19 pandemic period, the findings should be interpreted as temporal associations rather than causal effects. However, empirical findings linking absolute temperature levels to influenza incidence have been inconsistent across regions and time periods. analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在了解季节性热变化如何影响多个城市中流感 发病率 的表现,应对识别流感 暴发 模式中环境驱动因素变化的挑战。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究采用回顾性观察设计,将长期气候记录与短期流行病学时间序列相结合,聚焦于 1965–2025 年期间的北京、东京、纽约、伦敦和悉尼。流感病例与 COVID-19 病例分别分析,每日 发病率 使用 7 天移动平均进行平滑处理。
analysis_zh.methods: 每日流感 发病率 使用中心化的 7 天移动平均进行平滑处理,以减少高频噪声。通过皮尔逊相关分析,评估温度变化指标与流行病活动之间的关联,重点关注城市内部的时间共变性。相对湿度被作为补充的气候变量纳入分析,同样使用 7 天移动平均进行平滑处理,并分析其城市内部的时间共变性。
analysis_zh.main_results: 描述性分析显示,报告的流感 发病率 增加经常与快速升温、延迟降温以及与城市特定温度基准的更大偏离同时发生。绝对温度异常幅度显示出不太一致的独立关联,而降雪发现仍处于探索阶段。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者认为,热变化速率和与长期气候标准的偏离可能为描述流感活动时间提供补充信息,超越绝对温度单独的作用。

title: In Memoriam: The Enduring Influence of Nancy J. Cox (1948–2026)

full_text: Early Life and Scientific FoundationsNancy was born in rural Iowa in 1948 and earned a National Science Foundation scholarship to Iowa State University, completing her degree with highest honors. She then attended Cambridge University as a Marshall Scholar and entered the influenza field in the Division of Virology, Department of Pathology at Cambridge. Her early work examined molecular aspects of influenza virus replication, a foundation that shaped the rest of her career (2).Her focus on the fundamental biology of influenza viruses, especially how they evolved and interacted with the immune system, led her to understand how subtle genetic and antigenic differences affect epidemics. That insight contributed to one of her most enduring public health roles: guiding the selection of influenza viruses for use in the influenza vaccine. Nancy set the standards for how an influenza virus is characterized by using genomic and antigenic testing. As the head of a World Health Organization (WHO) Collaborating Center for Surveillance, Epidemiology, and Control of Influenza at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), she provided globally recognized leadership for the process used for preparing and selecting viruses for updating influenza vaccines.Over 37 years at CDC, Nancy helped transform a small team of scientists into the preeminent global center for influenza surveillance, epidemiology, research, and preparedness. She authored more than 278 scientific publications and helped define 3 pillars of modern influenza work: quantifying disease burden, characterizing emerging viruses, and using global systems for surveillance and response.There were 2 settings where Nancy was most comfortable in her professional life. The first was when she was diving deep into the testing of viruses. At weekly meetings, Nancy was always at the head of the table, often wearing a tailored suit jacket, and leading her staff as they reviewed detailed spreadsheets of virus test data. Such gatherings were an odd hybrid of cutting-edge biotechnology and priestly ritual, divining the future of each virus.The other setting was at small international meetings, where Nancy would engage in deep conversations on virus protein structure with colleagues during the day and then stay up late with the same friends sharing stories and recollections. Nancy understood that the best scientific collaborations were built not only on shared questions and rigorous methods but also on trust, respect, generosity, and genuine care for the people doing the work. Translating Virology into Public Health ActionNancy could see the connections between what a virus was doing in the laboratory and how those findings might affect global vaccine policy. She knew the science and she understood the politics. She could see how it all came together, from the genome in the laboratory to the geopolitical in Geneva. She integrated information across disciplines, spanning virus detection to disease prevention, and made it accessible and relevant for a comprehensive global influenza intelligence system.Nancy loved having things well-categorized, appropriately named, and understandable. She led the development of the Influenza Risk Assessment Tool, a structured framework for integrating virologic, epidemiologic, and population-level data to compare the pandemic potential of novel influenza A viruses (3). That framework has guided decision-making for novel influenza A viruses and reflects one of her signature approaches: moving from “what is this virus?” to “what should the world do about it?” Architect of Global Influenza Surveillance and Vaccine Virus SelectionIn 1992, Nancy became chief of CDC’s Influenza Branch and Director of the WHO Collaborating Center for Surveillance, Epidemiology, and Control of Influenza at CDC. In those roles, she strengthened WHO’s Global Influenza Surveillance and Response System (GISRS), a worldwide network of laboratories and public health institutions (4,5). Now comprising more than 160 National Influenza Centers in 136 countries and 7 Collaborating Centers, GISRS is the world’s main system for tracking influenza virus evolution in real time, selecting viruses for annual influenza vaccines and identifying viruses with pandemic potential (6).Nancy foresaw the importance of China’s development of influenza monitoring capacities because of the role of China and other countries in the region in the emergence of new influenza virus variants. Collaborating with WHO, she helped expand GISRS and build surveillance and response capabilities in many countries; these systems later proved fundamental during the COVID-19 pandemic. Her efforts expanded the global footprint of the CDC Influenza Division’s technical and funding support to national laboratories all around the world. That investment grew substantially over time to fill a critical gap in global surveillance and influenza prevention programs, and created an enduring trust of global partners in CDC, something Nancy championed as a requirement for collaborative responses to influenza threats.She also oversaw establishment of the Influenza Reagent Resource (later named the International Reagent Resource) to support manufacturing, stockpiling, and distribution of diagnostic reagents and test kits globally. This service fundamentally changed global surveillance by removing costs of core reagents and materials as a roadblock to robust surveillance systems.Nancy advanced modernization of influenza virus characterization methods. She promoted a “Seq-First” approach, in which genomic sequencing precedes traditional antigenic and serologic testing, enabling laboratories to expand evaluation of new variants for possible incorporation into seasonal influenza vaccines. Her focus on annual global and national vaccine strain selection, in partnership with WHO and the US Food and Drug Administration, was a key contribution to public health.Richard Hatchett, chief executive officer of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, stated, “Nancy was a giant and a tremendous advocate for science, public health, and international partnership. She played a huge role in establishing the international surveillance networks that protect us all, and her dedication to her work and to public service was immense.” Responding to Emerging ThreatsNancy’s career spanned the emergence of highly pathogenic avian influenza A(H5N1) in 1997 (7), the 2009 influenza A(H1N1) pandemic (8), and influenza A(H7N9) in China in 2013 (9). In those events, she helped define how animal influenza viruses can cross species barriers to humans, leading her to emphasize integration of animal and human surveillance, an approach central to contemporary One Health strategies.During the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, she guided US response policies, providing steadiness, clarity, and confidence, and serving as a trusted voice for public and private stakeholders. Her dedication and persistence shone clearly when, early in the pandemic response, her home was struck by lightning and burned down. When most people would have been near a breaking point, Nancy was still driving the response forward, focused on the outcome rather than the obstacle. Building Bridges through Influenza DiplomacyNancy believed in, and exemplified, CDC’s longstanding role of assisting countries around the world. She also believed that the United States and the international community were best served when scientific and public health knowledge, experience, and support were shared. She was recognized internationally as a uniquely authoritative and trusted influenza expert. WHO frequently sought her wisdom and assistance for critical activities, including development and evaluation of new Collaborating Centers, Pandemic Influenza Preparedness Framework negotiations, and international missions to assess complex situations such as influenza A(H7N9) in China and influenza A(H5N1) in Egypt.Dr. Margaret Chan, former director-general of WHO, wrote: “Your commitment, dedication, scientific attitude and quality of work has inspired everyone in the influenza community and has set an excellent example for the public health. We will miss your brilliant insights, unmatchable expertise, strong leadership and diplomatic skills, as well as your energy, dynamism and grace in our continuous defense against influenza threat.” Mentor and AdvocateNancy was a mentor and inspiration to scientists within her own team and around the world. Her scientific excellence, tireless work ethic, and collegial attitude inspired respect and admiration and provided a role model for young and senior scientists alike.Dr. Rebecca J. Garten Kondor, who has taken on the important role of guiding vaccine virus selection in CDC’s Influenza Division, recalled, “Early in my career I was fortunate to benefit from Nancy’s leadership and mentorship, where I learned the value of bringing multiple disciplines to the table and setting high standards of scientific rigor and integrity. Getting it right—and having confidence in our results—is essential because CDC science is widely respected, and sharing our analysis capabilities and know-how with global partners strengthens influenza surveillance and pandemic preparedness.”Professor Yoshi Kawaoka stated, “So much of my career has been influenced by your work. You leave behind a wonderful footprint — you have touched the lives of and will be missed by many.” Professor Guan Yi, University of Hong Kong, China, called her “a scientist of extraordinary vision, a tireless diplomat of public health, and a deeply cherished friend and mentor to so many of us in the global influenza research community.”Upon Nancy’s retirement in 2014, then-Senator Tom Harkin (D-Iowa) honored her by stating in the Congressional Record, “During her 37 years at CDC, Dr. Cox has served as mentor, educator, supervisor, and supporter to hundreds of individuals: undergraduates, medical and PhD students, postdoctoral fellows, laboratory and epidemiology staff members, journalists, and visiting researchers” (10). Recognition and Enduring LegacyNancy was referred to as a “walking encyclopedia of influenza,” and her knowledge of influenza was legendary. She fostered a culture of high quality, scientific excellence, mutual respect, and accountability, and led through example. One former colleague said, “She held our feet to scientific fire, only because she could walk across those coals.” Nancy spent her career raising the bar for scientific excellence, an approach needed now more than ever.Nancy received numerous awards, including the Samuel J. Heyman Service to America Medal as Federal Employee of the Year in 2006 and recognition by Time magazine as one of the 100 most influential people of 2006. Dr. Anthony Fauci, former Director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases at the National Institutes of Health, considered her “one of the leading figures in the influenza research community,” whose work “benefitted millions of Americans and people around the world.”Professionally, her legacy is reflected in the systems she helped build: global surveillance networks, vaccine selection processes, and preparedness frameworks that continue to protect populations worldwide. Personally, among those privileged to know and work with her, the deepest impression is her legacy of warmth, generosity, fairness, inclusiveness, and commitment to public health.Dr. Nancy Cox died on April 23, 2026. She is survived by her husband, daughter, her granddaughter, stepson and wife, three step-grandchildren, and other family members.

Taponamiento cardíaco por influenza A: reporte de un caso de manejo médico, sin drenaje pericárdico. Crónicas Científicas. 2026;30(3):35-40. doi:10.55139/ZIVM4883. Resumen El taponamiento cardíaco es una complicación infrecuente de la influenza A, como consecuencia de miopericarditis o pericarditis. A pesar de ser potencialmente mortal, el manejo puede individualizarse según criterios clínicos, ecocardiográficos y hemodinámicos, optando entre pericardiocentesis inmediata o manejo médico. Se presenta el caso clínico de un paciente de 60 años que consulta al servicio de emergencias por dolor torácico, disnea y síncope, con síntomas respiratorios de dos semanas de evolución. Se documentó un derrame pericárdico y posteriormente un ecocardiograma confirmó taponamiento cardíaco secundario a miopericarditis, atribuida a influenza A. Dado el riesgo hemorrágico asociado a la anticoagulación recibida como parte del manejo inicial, se difirió la pericardiocentesis y se optó por vigilancia estrecha. Durante la evolución, el paciente presentó datos de shock, que requirió optimización de volumen y vasopresores; sin embargo, dada la persistencia de la contraindicación para el drenaje, se mantuvo el manejo médico conservador, logrando resolución completa del taponamiento sin necesidad de intervención invasiva. Este caso demuestra la viabilidad del manejo médico individualizado en pacientes con taponamiento cardíaco cuidadosamente seleccionados según sus características clínicas y perfil de riesgo. Palabras claves Taponamiento cardíaco, Gripe humana, Derrame pericárdico, Miocarditis, Pericarditis, Tratamiento conservador, Informe de casos, Costa Rica. Abstract Cardiac tamponade is an infrequent complication of influenza A, occurring as a consequence of myopericarditis or pericarditis. Although potentially life-threatening, its management can be individualized based on clinical, echocardiographic, and hemodynamic criteria, with options ranging from immediate pericardiocentesis to medical management. We present the case of a 60-year-old patient who presented to the emergency department with chest pain, dyspnea, and a syncopal episode, following a two weeks history of respiratory symptoms. A pericardial effusion was documented, and a subsequent echocardiogram confirmed cardiac tamponade secondary to myopericarditis attributed to influenza A. Given the hemorrhagic risk associated with anticoagulation administered as part of the initial management, pericardiocentesis was deferred and close monitoring was chosen instead. During the clinical course, the patient developed signs of shock, requiring volume optimization and vasopressor support. However, given the persistence of the contraindication to drainage, conservative medical management was maintained, achieving complete resolution of the tamponade without the need for invasive intervention. This case illustrates the feasibility of individualized medical management in carefully selected patients with cardiac tamponade, based on their clinical characteristics and risk profile. Resumen El taponamiento cardíaco es una complicación infrecuente de la influenza A, como consecuencia de miopericarditis o pericarditis. A pesar de ser potencialmente mortal, el manejo puede individualizarse según criterios clínicos, ecocardiográficos y hemodinámicos, optando entre pericardiocentesis inmediata o manejo médico. Se presenta el caso clínico de un paciente de 60 años que consulta al servicio de emergencias por dolor torácico, disnea y síncope, con síntomas respiratorios de dos semanas de evolución. Se documentó un derrame pericárdico y posteriormente un ecocardiograma confirmó taponamiento cardíaco secundario a miopericarditis, atribuida a influenza A. Dado el riesgo hemorrágico asociado a la anticoagulación recibida como parte del manejo inicial, se difirió la pericardiocentesis y se optó por vigilancia estrecha. Durante la evolución, el paciente presentó datos de shock, que requirió optimización de volumen y vasopresores; sin embargo, dada la persistencia de la contraindicación para el drenaje, se mantuvo el manejo médico conservador, logrando resolución completa del taponamiento sin necesidad de intervención invasiva. Este caso demuestra la viabilidad del manejo médico individualizado en pacientes con taponamiento cardíaco cuidadosamente seleccionados según sus características clínicas y perfil de riesgo. Abstract Cardiac tamponade is an infrequent complication of influenza A, occurring as a consequence of myopericarditis or pericarditis. Although potentially life-threatening, its management can be individualized based on clinical, echocardiographic, and hemodynamic criteria, with options ranging from immediate pericardiocentesis to medical management. We present the case of a 60-year-old patient who presented to the emergency department with chest pain, dyspnea, and a syncopal episode, following a two weeks history of respiratory symptoms. A pericardial effusion was documented, and a subsequent echocardiogram confirmed cardiac tamponade secondary to myopericarditis attributed to influenza A. Given the hemorrhagic risk associated with anticoagulation administered as part of the initial management, pericardiocentesis was deferred and close monitoring was chosen instead. During the clinical course, the patient developed signs of shock, requiring volume optimization and vasopressor support. However, given the persistence of the contraindication to drainage, conservative medical management was maintained, achieving complete resolution of the tamponade without the need for invasive intervention. This case illustrates the feasibility of individualized medical management in carefully selected patients with cardiac tamponade, based on their clinical characteristics and risk profile.
